subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is a partially double‑stranded DNA virus that infects hepatocytes, causing acute and chronic liver disease and increasing hepatocellular carcinoma risk.

sections.p: HBV is a small enveloped virus (≈42 nm) with a partially double‑stranded DNA genome and a reverse‑transcribing polymerase. It targets liver cells and can persist for decades.
b: Key protein: surface antigen (HBsAg) used for vaccine

sections.p: The virus enters hepatocytes via the sodium‑taurocholate cotransporting polypeptide (NTCP) receptor, then releases its relaxed circular DNA, which is converted to covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA) in the nucleus.
b: cccDNA acts as a stable template for viral transcription
Reverse transcriptase makes new DNA from an RNA intermediate

sections.p: HBV spreads through blood and body fluids; the virus is stable outside the body for up to 7 days, allowing horizontal transmission in low‑resource settings.
b: Perinatal, sexual, percutaneous, and unsafe injections
Survives on surfaces, needles, and medical equipment

t.b: Is the patient currently infected? Positive indicates acute or chronic infection
Is this an acute infection? IgM positivity points to recent exposure
What is the viral load? High levels guide treatment decisions; if unavailable, use ALT and HBeAg status as surrogate

sections.p: HBV infection presents as a spectrum: asymptomatic acute illness, symptomatic acute hepatitis, or chronic infection that can progress to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
b: Acute phase: jaundice, fatigue, RUQ pain; usually self‑limited
Chronic infection: defined by HBsAg >6 months; risk of cirrhosis ~20 % and HCC ~5 % over 20 years
Immune‑tolerant, immune‑active, inactive carrier, and reactivation phases guide management

sections.p: Serologic profiling combined with viral load quantification determines infection stage and need for therapy.
b: HBeAg positivity + high HBV DNA → active replication
ALT >2 × ULN with HBV DNA >20 000 IU/mL → treatment indication

t.b: Has the patient been immunised or cleared infection? Positive indicates immunity
Is the virus actively replicating? Positive correlates with high viral load
Is there evidence of HCC? Nodules + elevated AFP suggest cancer

sections.p: Therapy aims to suppress viral replication, prevent liver damage, and reduce HCC risk. First‑line agents are nucleos(t)ide analogues with high barrier to resistance.
b: Entecavir or tenofovir: potent, low resistance, safe in pregnancy
Avoid lamivudine monotherapy due to rapid resistance
Vaccination (HBsAg) for prevention; birth‑dose crucial in endemic areas

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams and clinical reasoning.
b: HBV is a dsDNA virus with reverse transcriptase – unique among hepatitis viruses
Chronic infection defined by HBsAg >6 months
Treatment indicated when ALT >2 × ULN and HBV DNA >20 000 IU/mL in immune‑active phase

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden rise in bilirubin with hepatic encephalopathy

faq.a: Current antivirals suppress replication but do not eradicate cccDNA; functional cure (loss of HBsAg) is rare.

faq.q: Why is the birth‑dose vaccine important?
faq.a: Most chronic infections arise from perinatal exposure; a timely vaccine prevents 90 % of vertical transmission.

faq.q: How does HBV differ from HCV?
faq.a: HBV is a DNA virus with a vaccine; HCV is an RNA virus, no vaccine, and treatment relies on direct‑acting antivirals.

exam: Explain the serologic pattern that distinguishes acute, chronic, and resolved HBV infection.
Describe the criteria for initiating antiviral therapy in chronic HBV.
List the major routes of HBV transmission and preventive measures in low‑resource settings.
